Demo 2 shows the pattern: the output is a 2x2 tiling of transformed versions of the input — top-left = original, top-right = column-reversed transpose, bottom-left = row-reversed transpose, bottom-right = 180° rotation. I verified this against demo 1's first row too.

```python
def transform(grid):
    A = [row[:] for row in grid]
    n = len(A)
    T = [[A[j][i] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]  # transpose
    B = [row[::-1] for row in T]        # reverse columns of transpose
    C = B[::-1]                         # reverse rows of transpose
    D = [row[::-1] for row in A[::-1]]  # rot180
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(A[i] + B[i])
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(C[i] + D[i])
    return out
```

{"action": "submit"}

The top half was correct; the bottom-left quadrant differs. Comparing demo 2: bottom-left rows equal columns of the input read top-to-bottom in right-to-left order (C[i] = column n-1-i), while top-right B[i] = column i read bottom-to-top, and bottom-right is the 180° rotation. Verified on demo 1 (e.g., row 14 = column 11 top-down).

```python
def transform(grid):
    A = [row[:] for row in grid]
    n = len(A)
    B = [[A[n-1-j][i] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]      # col i, bottom-up
    C = [[A[j][n-1-i] for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]      # col n-1-i, top-down
    D = [row[::-1] for row in A[::-1]]                            # rot180
    out = [A[i] + B[i] for i in range(n)] + [C[i] + D[i] for i in range(n)]
    return out
```
